transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-03-22
Start time: 17:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Maya Thompson (Redwood AE), Daniel Park (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (CTO, Cerulean), Alex Reed (Eng Mgr, Cerulean), Priya Singh (SRE, Cerulean)

Auto Summary (auto-generated, may be fuzzy):
Cerulean evaluating Redwood options (Hosted, Dedicated, Private) focused on reliability during partial degradations. Key topics: multi-region routing, fallback to smaller/cheaper models, SLA expectations during degraded network, audit logs and KMS requirements. Action: Redwood to send pricing and plan for benchmarking.

Topics: reliability expectations; fallback policy; multi-region routing; SLA mapping; private deploy constraints; benchmarks.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya, I'm the account lead on this. Daniel from our solutions engineering team will cover technical bits. Jordan, Alex, Priya, thanks for making time. Sound good?
[00:12] Jordan (Cerulean CTO): Yep, thanks. We've heard good things about Redwood's inference economics so excited to dig in.
[00:18] Alex (Cerulean): Quick note, I'm coming from the eng side. Primary concerns are predictable latency and what happens if a region goes noisy.
[00:26] Priya (SRE): And for us, the oncall team's worried about cascade failures — we need clear fallbacks and observability.
[00:32] Daniel (Redwood SE): Great, we built a couple of patterns for that — policy-driven routing, auto-fallback to model variants, and region steering. We'll walk through specifics.
[00:42] Maya: I'll hand to Daniel for a short tech overview, then we'll map to your failure modes and SLAs.

[00:47] Daniel: Cool. I'll be a bit colloquial — apologies for transcription, my accent gets squashed sometimes. So, at a high-level: Redwood supports Hosted, Dedicated, and Private. For reliability we recommend a layered fallback approach: 1) local cache + prefix KV, 2) degrade model size (e.g., from rdx-large -> rdx-medium), 3) regional failover, 4) queued background processing for async work. Each layer trades latency, cost, and fidelity.
[01:18] Jordan: When you say "degrade model size" do you mean a different model family or a quantized variant? Can you do automatic fallback?
[01:26] Daniel: Both. We have model variants we curate — some are quantized, some are distilled. Fallback can be policy-based: e.g., if p95 latency > 350ms or error rate > 3% for two minutes, route to the variant. You can pin per-route policies.
[01:40] Alex: How much of the state is preserved, like KV cache/embedding cache, when you fallback between variants? We don't want the context to blow away.
[01:49] Daniel: Good question. KV caches are per-model-architecture family — switching from the same family but lower capacity usually preserves most of the warm cache. If you move to a different architecture, cache warm-up is required. We also support prefix caching at the application layer which persists across variants.
[02:03] Priya: Our priority is availability over perfect outputs — so switching architecture is ok if we can bound user-visible regressions. Do you have quality-regression tooling?
[02:11] Daniel: Yes, Redwood Optimize can run evals on your prompt set and flag regressions under target metrics. We'll include that in the pilot.

[02:20] Maya: I want to surface two common enterprise asks: 1) If we deploy Dedicated, what's the SLA during partial hardware or AZ outages? 2) For Private, how much control do they get over traffic steering?
[02:32] Daniel: For Dedicated we offer a capacity-backed SLA — throughput and 99th latency targets per commit tier. In partial AZ loss, we have node-level redundancy and automated rebalancing; if capacity dips below your commit we'll trigger fallback to Hosted with encryption in transit — assuming you enabled cross-tier fallback in policy.
[02:49] Jordan: So you can failover to Hosted as an escape hatch? That makes legal nervous — data residency, encryption, and audit must be preserved.
[02:58] Maya: Yeah that's common. We keep data residency constraints in mind: cross-tier fallback is opt-in and we document data flows. For Private-only customers we can do regional standby or multi-site Private deployments rather than go Hosted.
[03:12] Alex: Private multi-site — is that the on-prem package or VPC in multiple regions?
[03:17] Daniel: Both. We have a private control plane and can set up identical stacks in two regions or one on-prem + one cloud. Traffic steering is via our routing policy — can be latency-based, region-pref, or manual.
[03:28] Priya: What's observability look like during a failover? We want token-level cost, per-route latency, and an audit trail for who triggered policies.
[03:37] Daniel: Console emits per-request traces with model variant, route decision, and any fallback trigger reason. Audit logs are available to download or stream to your SIEM. We also integrate with KMS/HSM for keying and send audit records to your S3 or vendor logs.
[03:51] Jordan: Is SSO/SAML available for operators?
[03:54] Maya: Yes, SSO, RBAC, and SCIM for provisioning. For Private, you can hook into your identity provider.

[04:01] Alex: Let's talk about concrete failure scenarios — say a regional networking blip that increases p99 by 400ms for 10 minutes. What's the typical play?
[04:10] Daniel: You can set a dynamic policy: if p99 > X ms for Y minutes, ramp model fallback and then region steer. For user-facing low-latency routes we recommend keeping a low-latency variant in a second region as hot standby. For noncritical batch tasks, we queue and process later.
[04:27] Priya: How fast does model variant warm-up happen? We can't accept minutes of cold-start where requests time out.
[04:33] Daniel: For hot standby we keep a small pool warm — warm-up time is seconds for KV preserved variants; for cold spin-ups we suggest warm-replica pre-provisioning. Autoscaling can be aggressive but provisioning a GPU-backed replica takes tens of seconds depending on underlying infra.
[04:51] Jordan: That "tens of seconds" is a problem for our chat critical path. Could we do a cross-region traffic split with gradual ramp to avoid a sudden spike?
[04:59] Daniel: Absolutely — traffic-splitting with gradual ramp and canary verification reduces spike risk. Our routing supports percentage splits and automatic rollback if error rates climb.
[05:10] Maya: Jordan — what's your tolerance for brief increases in latency versus incomplete responses? Do you prefer longer tails or losing fidelity?
[05:18] Jordan: We prefer latency over bad hallucinations. Users expect a timely answer; if it's not confident, we can fall back to a short canned response. But we need SLA clauses for this.
[05:27] Alex: Related, our legal team asked about SLA credits during regional degradations and what constitutes "service outage" — is degraded performance considered an outage?
[05:36] Maya: Typically SLA definitions include availability and latency targets. Degradation that keeps service functional but over target is usually an SLA breach for latency metrics, but not full availability outage. We can map specific p95/p99 thresholds to credits.
[05:50] Daniel: We can show examples: Dedicated tier X has 99.9% uptime and p95 < 250ms for text-gen. During partial regional loss, we offer fallback behavior and we document what conditions trigger credits.

[06:03] Priya: About security: do you support customer-managed keys and HSM? We require that for Private.
[06:08] Daniel: Yes, KMS/HSM integrations are supported for Private and Dedicated. Hosted can support customer-supplied keys via Bring-Your-Own-Key integrations depending on region and contract.
[06:19] Jordan: And audit logs retention can be configured? We may need 7 years for compliance.
[06:24] Maya: We have add-on retention tiers; multi-year retention is available through the Enterprise package. We'll include that in the follow-up.

[06:34] Alex: Let's do a micro-scenario: traffic surge in EU region + region-level network partition that prevents reaching one availability zone. How does the request path look?
[06:44] Daniel: Request comes to the EU ingress, load balancer sees increased latency, routing policy marks region degraded, traffic is gradually steered to secondary EU region or to US hot standby (if allowed). At the same time, local cache handles repetitive prompts which reduces load. If your Dedicated commit is still under threshold we won't spill to Hosted. If the commit is saturated we have two options: 1) automatic split to Hosted fallback, 2) shed noncritical workloads and prioritize critical routes. Policies decide precedence.
[07:09] Priya: Will the logs show which policy caused the steer so we can triage postmortem?
[07:13] Daniel: Yes, each decision is tagged with a reason code and a policy ID; we expose that in traces.

[07:20] Jordan: Cost — steering to Hosted during incidents could explode cost. How do we manage that?
[07:25] Maya: We recommend budgeting for incident runbook: e.g., define a dollar cap for cross-tier fallback or enable rate-limiting on noncritical routes. We can set per-route spend caps.
[07:35] Alex: Ok. For the pilot, we'd like to validate two things: 1) failover correctness for region outage, 2) performance delta when falling back to quantized models.
[07:44] Daniel: Perfect. A small benchmark suite with your prompts will cover that. We'll run end-to-end tests: simulate AZ outage, measure p95/p99, and inspect quality regressions.

[07:52] Priya: One subtlety — our product often chains multiple calls where latency compounds. Any suggestions for guarding the chain?
[07:59] Daniel: Use local short-circuit cache for repeated intermediate outputs, and we support synchronous short-circuit responses with a "best-effort" flag. Also you can mark steps as nonblocking and queue them if downstream is degraded.

[08:12] Jordan: About change management: if we adopt Dedicated, how are model upgrades handled safely? We need canary and rollback.
[08:19] Daniel: We support canary rollouts across a percentage of traffic by route, plus automatic rollback triggers on quality/regression signals. Rollouts are plannable and auditable.
[08:30] Alex: Does Redwood publish benchmark numbers for the curated models? We want realistic expectations.
[08:35] Maya: We have a model catalog with empirical perf profiles across sequence lengths and hardware. We'll attach a couple of sample PDFs.

[08:43] Jordan: Onboarding: what's typical pilot length to claim readiness for prod?
[08:48] Maya: Usually 4-6 weeks: week 1 integration and sample prompts, weeks 2-3 benchmarking and SLO tuning, weeks 4-6 pilot with production traffic and runbook dry-runs. For larger Private deployments add provisioning lead time.
[08:59] Priya: Lead times — Dedicated GPU fleet provisioning times?
[09:03] Daniel: Depends on region and commit; small reserved pools can be 1-2 weeks; larger multi-AZ fleets potentially months if specific GPU types are required. We'll give a timeline per your capacity needs.

[09:15] Alex: A few pragmatic asks from our ops team: 1) a simple JSON policy language we can version-control, 2) playbooks for typical incidents, 3) runbook example for cross-region failover.
[09:26] Daniel: We have a policy DSL that is JSON/YAML friendly; we'll share examples. We also have runbook templates we can adapt.

[09:34] Jordan: Anything we should be worried about that customers usually forget?
[09:37] Maya: Two things: 1) traffic shaping during rollouts to avoid cold-start spikes, and 2) housekeeping for cache TTLs so your prefix caches don't saturate memory during big bursts.
[09:47] Priya: On cache TTLs, is there a recommended default?
[09:50] Daniel: Defaults are conservative (minutes to hours) but depend on your prompt repetition profile. For chat contexts we usually keep short TTLs and rely on prefix compression for longer lived context.

[09:59] Alex: Let's capture acceptance criteria for pilot: 1) failover completes within X seconds with less than Y% error increase, 2) p95 within 1.5x baseline when on fallback variant, 3) audit logs and KMS flow validated.
[10:12] Maya: I'll write these up and push to the ticket.

[10:18] Daniel: Quick note — our "fallback policy matrix" example can be applied per-route and we're happy to make one tailored to your critical endpoints.
[10:25] Jordan: Sounds good. Any final compliance gaps we should be aware of? We mentioned long-term log retention, and also need EU data residency if we use EU-hosted models.
[10:35] Maya: Data residency is configurable for Private and Dedicated. For Hosted we have EU regions; cross-tier fallback is opt-in and will be called out in the data flow. We'll include a diagram.

[10:44] Alex: Let's do the next steps: share pricing + retention appendix; get a benchmarking slot; Cerulean to send traffic profile.
[10:52] Maya: Noted. We'll also include a sample runbook and the policy DSL snippet.

[10:58] Jordan: Thanks. One last quick Q — do you have references from customers who ran similar regional failover tests?
[11:03] Maya: Yes, we'll share two anonymized references and a short case note.

[11:08] Priya: Great. That covers it for us.
[11:12] Maya: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the materials and a proposed bench slot.

[11:17] End meeting.

Post-call notes (auto):
- Customer priority: availability-first with bounded quality degradation rather than silent failures.
- Main risks: cross-tier fallback cost, cache warm-up during variant switch, Dedicated provisioning lead time.
